description: Two hundred eighty-one scholars of American history filed a brief in Webster v. Reproductive Health Services, a case that rejected a constitutional challenge to Missouri legislation that placed restrictions on abortions. The brief explains that abortion was legal and widely accessible throughout the 18th and 19th centuries, and that historical restrictions on abortion were grounded in rationales that have become “anachronistic or constitutionally and culturally impermissible.” The brief urges the Court to consider whether the “protection of unborn life has become a surrogate” for those outmoded rationales. In making their argument, the amici emphasize a shift in American historical inquiry since Roe v. Wade (1973) away from “the study of wars, formal legal rules, economics and elections to . . . a fuller and more rounded account of American social history.”
title: Webster v. Reproductive Health Services (1989)
brief_title: Brief of 281 American Historians as Amici Curiae Supporting Appellees
tags: Reproductive Rights, Abortion Care, 14th Amendment, Equal Protection Clause, Due Process Clause, Privacy

description: Two hundred fifty scholars of American history filed a brief in Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey, a case that introduced an “undue burden” standard for evaluating the constitutionality of abortion restrictions. The brief — which is similar in substance to the historians’ brief filed in Webster v. Reproductive Health Services (1989) — argues that a woman’s right to abortion is consistent with the nation’s history and tradition. The amici explain that abortion has been tolerated and legal for much of the nation’s history; any claim that “abortion restrictions enjoyed broad social support in past eras,” they contend, is historically inaccurate.
title: Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey (1992)
brief_title: Brief of 250 American Historians as Amici Curiae in Support of Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania
tags: Reproductive Rights, Abortion Care, 14th Amendment, Equal Protection Clause, Due Process Clause, Privacy

description: Sixteen historians whose research focuses on the lives of women filed a brief in Whole Woman’s Health v. Hellerstedt, a case that invalidated a Texas law requiring abortion providers to have admitting privileges at local hospitals, and requiring abortion facilities to meet the standards applied to ambulatory surgical centers. The brief argues that the statute in question was part of a long tradition of laws rooted in the paternalistic doctrine of coverture, which the courts have previously struck down as unconstitutional sex discrimination. The amici urge the Supreme Court to scrutinize the law carefully to determine whether it actually promoted women’s health and at what cost to women’s liberty. They emphasized that laws of this kind typically mask gender stereotypes that subordinate and harm women under the pretense of protecting them.
title: Whole Woman’s Health v. Hellerstedt (2016)
brief_title: Brief of Historians as Amici Curiae in Support of Petitioners
tags: Reproductive Rights, Abortion Care, 14th Amendment

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which ruled that the Constitution does not provide a right to abortion and overruled both Roe v. Wade (1973) and Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey (1992). The American Historical Association and the Organization of American Historians jointly submitted a brief in support of abortion providers. The brief describes the history of abortion regulations from English common law through the end of the 19th century to demonstrate that American history and tradition include a woman’s ability to make decisions regarding abortion. Among other things, the amici explain that English common law — which did not recognize or regulate abortion until quickening (i.e., when a pregnant woman first feels fetal movement) — influenced U.S. state laws prior to the 14th Amendment’s ratification in 1868. At that time, the brief shows, nearly half of the states allowed pre-quickening abortions or imposed lighter punishments for them. The American Society for Legal History and 23 historians with expertise in the law, history, and politics of reproduction filed a brief in support of abortion providers. According to the amici, claims that Roe “drove the division and polarization around abortion” are historically inaccurate. The brief explores developments straddling the Court’s issuance of Roe to demonstrate that conflicts misattributed by right-wing lawyers to Roe either predated that decision or emerged later in response to other forces, such as the realignment of political parties in the late 20th century.
title: Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022)
brief_title: Brief for Amici Curiae American Historical Association and Organization of American Historians in Support of Respondents | Brief for Amici Curiae American Society for Legal History and Other Scholars with Expertise in the Law, History and Politics of Reproduction in the United States in Support of Respondents
tags: Reproductive Rights, Abortion Care, 14th Amendment, Due Process Clause

description: Ten historians and scholars of gender and sexuality filed a brief in Lawrence v. Texas, which ruled that a Texas law criminalizing sexual intimacy by same-sex couples violated the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause. Arguing in support of invalidating laws like Texas’s, the brief underscores that government regulation of sexual activity between members of the same sex lacks a deep historical pedigree, and that government policies discriminating against people based on their sexual orientation are part of a distinctly 20th-century project that was already being dismantled at the time of the case.
title: Lawrence v. Texas (2003)
brief_title: Brief of Professors of History George Chauncey, Nancy F. Cott, John D’Emilio, Estelle B. Freedman, Thomas C. Holt, John Howard, Lynn Hunt, Mark D. Jordan, Elizabeth Lapovsky Kennedy, and Linda P. Kerber as Amici Curiae in Support of Petitioners
tags: LGBTQ+, Sexual Orientation/Gender Identity Discrimination, 14th Amendment, Due Process Clause

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in United States v. Windsor, which ruled the 1996 Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) unconstitutional for denying legally married same-sex couples equal protection under the Fifth Amendment. The Organization of American Historians and the American Studies Association filed a brief in support of DOMA’s challengers. The brief presents the long history of discrimination faced by gay and lesbian people since the founding era and into the 21st century. It concludes with a discussion of Supreme Court case law to underscore the significance that the Court has long accorded to history in assessing equal protection claims. The American Historical Association and 23 historians of American marriage, family, and law also filed a brief in support of DOMA’s challengers. The brief argues that DOMA “breaks with historical understanding of the state and federal roles with respect to marriage,” under which the states — rather than the federal government — have defined marriage status. It also explains that the states have recognized many different purposes for marriage throughout the nation’s history.
title: United States v. Windsor (2013)

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Hollingsworth v. Perry, which ruled that same-sex couples lacked the legal standing to challenge a California proposition limiting the state’s official definition of marriage to a union between a man and a woman. The Organization of American Historians filed a brief supporting the challenge to the proposition on 14th Amendment grounds. Similar to the historians’ brief filed in United States v. Windsor (2013), this brief recounts the long history of discrimination faced by gay and lesbian people since the founding era. It concludes with a discussion of Supreme Court case law to underscore the significance that the Court has long accorded to history in assessing equal protection claims. Nineteen scholars of history and other disciplines filed a brief supporting the legality of the California proposition. The brief argues that the United States lacks a “deeply rooted history, legal tradition, or practice of gay marriage,” and that marriage has historically been “an opposite-sex institution” because it serves “child-centered purposes.” Amicus Curiae Brief of Scholars of History and Related Disciplines in Support of Petitioners
title: Hollingsworth v. Perry (2013)
brief_title: Brief of the Organization of American Historians and the American Studies Association as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Obergefell v. Hodges, the case that established same-sex couples’ 14th Amendment right to marry and ruled that states must recognize same-sex marriages performed in other states. The Organization of American Historians filed a brief in support of same-sex marriage as a constitutionally conferred right. Like the historians’ briefs filed in United States v. Windsor (2013) and Hollingsworth v. Perry (2013), this brief presents the long history of discrimination that same-sex couples have faced from the founding era through the present. It also explains that this history should trigger heightened scrutiny of the state law at issue, in keeping with the Court’s long-standing equal protection jurisprudence. The American Historical Association and 26 historians of marriage, family, and law filed a brief in support of the constitutionality of same-sex marriage. According to the amici, the historical record demonstrates that procreation and child-rearing have never been the exclusive or even predominant purpose of marriage. The brief also surveys historical American marriage laws to show that marriage is not a static concept, but rather one that has evolved over time “to reflect societal changes and judicial recognition of legal rights.” Eleven scholars of history and related disciplines filed a brief challenging the right to same-sex marriage. The brief argues that the “traditional” definition of marriage (i.e., a relationship between a man and a woman) is dominant in the country’s history, tradition, and practice, reflecting the institution’s purported purpose of supporting procreation and child-rearing. For these reasons, the amici maintain, restrictions on same-sex marriage are rational and constitutional.
title: Obergefell v. Hodges (2015)
brief_title: Brief of the Organization of American Historians as Amicus Curiae in Support of Petitioners | Brief of Historians of Marriage and the American Historical Association as Amici Curiae in Support of Petitioners | Brief of Amici Curiae Scholars of History and Related Disciplines in Support of Respondents

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Bostock v. Clayton County, Georgia and related cases that ruled firing someone for being gay or transgender a violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination against individuals “because of” their sex. Nine historians with expertise in the history of gender, sexuality, and law in the United States filed a brief supporting an interpretation of Title VII that protects people against discrimination because they are lesbian, gay, bisexual, or transgender. The brief describes how historical evidence from the first decade after Title VII’s enactment illustrates that the public understanding of the word sex and of the phrase “discrimination because of . . . sex” encompassed discrimination against LGBTQ+ individuals. The statute, the amici further explain, sought to support people who “depart from conventional norms of masculinity and femininity.” Thirty-eight scholars of LGBTQ+ rights and history filed a brief supporting a reading of Title VII that protects transgender people from discrimination. The brief argues that the plain text of Title VII should be sufficient to conclude that discrimination because a person is transgender is legally barred. The amici further explain that the legislative record does not indicate congressional intent to exclude transgender individuals from Title VII’s protections.
title: Bostock v. Clayton County, Georgia (2020); Altitude Express, Inc. v. Zarda (2020); R. G. & G. R. Harris Funeral Homes, Inc. v. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (2018)
brief_title: Brief of Historians as Amici Curiae in Support of Employees | Brief of Law and History Professors as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondent Aimee Stephens
tags: LGBTQ+, Sexual Orientation/Gender Identity Discrimination, Civil Rights Law

description: Seven historians of child welfare filed a brief in Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, which held that the City of Philadelphia’s policy of requiring foster care agencies to certify that they would not discriminate against same-sex couples violated the agencies’ rights under the Free Exercise Clause. The brief, filed in support of the policy, explains that governments have regulated child welfare since the country’s founding. Among other things, the amici describe how the government grew substantially more involved in funding and regulating foster care over the past century — developing standards and systems of licensure to both ensure the adequate protection of minor children and guard against discrimination by private entities in the foster care system.
title: Fulton v. City of Philadelphia (2021)
brief_title: Brief of Historians of Child Welfare as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: LGBTQ+, Sexual Orientation/Gender Identity Discrimination, First Amendment, Free Exercise Clause

description: The American Historical Association, the Organization of American Historians, the LGBTQ+ History Association, and eight historians with expertise in the history of gender, sexuality, and medicine filed a brief in United States v. Skrmetti, a case that considered whether a Tennessee bill restricting certain medical treatments for transgender minors violated the 14th Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause. The brief, filed in support of the transgender minors’ right to receive treatment, explains that the medical diagnosis of gender dysphoria has been recognized, treated, and relieved through gender-affirming medical interventions for centuries. The amici contend that the medical interventions threatened by the Tennessee bill, which include surgery and hormone therapy, are “well-established, mainstream forms of health care” with deep historical pedigrees.
title: United States v. Skrmetti (2025)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae American Historical Association, Organization of American Historians, LGBTQ+ History Association, and Historian Scholars in Support of Petitioner and Respondents in Support of Petitioner
tags: 14th Amendment, Equal Protection Clause, Gender-Affirming Care

description: Eight scholars of history, political science, and law who specialize in the history of citizenship and gender filed a brief in Flores-Villar v. United States, a case that considered a constitutional challenge to federal statutory conditions under which children born abroad can claim U.S. citizenship. At the time of the challenge, federal law had different requirements for unwed American mothers and fathers to pass citizenship to a child born outside the United States. The brief argues that federal laws governing citizenship transmission have reflected sex-based stereotypes and outdated gender norms since the founding era.
title: Flores-Villar v. United States (2011)
brief_title: Brief Amici Curiae of Professors of History, Political Science, and Law in Support of Petitioner
tags: Immigration, Citizenship, Gender, Fifth Amendment, Equal Protection Clause

description: Thirteen scholars of history, law, and political science with expertise in the history of citizenship and gender filed a brief in Sessions v. Morales-Santana, which invalidated a federal statute that treated unwed American fathers and mothers differently for purposes of passing citizenship to children born abroad. The brief canvasses historical citizenship laws to demonstrate the federal government’s pattern of relying on “outdated gender-based norms concerning proper parental roles” to regulate citizenship transmission. The amici maintain that laws of this kind contradict the Supreme Court’s equal protection and due process principles.
title: Sessions v. Morales-Santana (2017)
brief_title: Brief Amici Curiae of Professors of History, Political Science, and Law in Support of Respondent
tags: Immigration, Citizenship, Gender, Fifth Amendment, Equal Protection Clause

description: Six historians and social scientists filed an brief in Department of Commerce v. New York, a case in which the Supreme Court blocked the Commerce Department’s decision to add a citizenship question to the 2020 census. The brief challenges the Commerce Department’s claim that its decision was merely a “reinstatement” of a question “whose pedigree dates back nearly 200 years.” The amici explain that the census has never asked for the citizenship status of everyone in the country, and that, more importantly, the census has changed in material ways that limit older iterations’ usefulness as models for contemporary ones.
title: Department of Commerce v. New York (2019)
brief_title: Brief of Historians and Social Scientists Margo Anderson, Andrew Beveridge, Rachel Buff, Morgan Kousser, Mae Ngai, and Steven Ruggles as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: Citizenship, Census, Democracy

description: The American Historical Association, the Organization of American Historians, and 42 historians filed a brief in Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, which ruled that the decision by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to rescind the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) policy violated the Administrative Procedure Act. The brief, filed in support of DACA, illustrates how government officials have used seemingly race-neutral language to hide discriminatory motivations and communicate racial and political messages over the course of U.S. history. The amici apply a widely accepted methodology called code word analysis to elucidate the anti-Mexican and anti-Latino sentiment underlying DHS’s decision. Amici Curiae Brief of American Historical Association, Organization of American Historians, 42 Historians, and the Fred T. Korematsu Center for Law and Equality in Support of Respondents
title: Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California (2020)
tags: Immigration, Fifth Amendment, Equal Protection

description: Eleven historians and social scientists with expertise covering the census and immigration filed a brief in Trump v. New York, a case involving a constitutional challenge to a 2020 executive order that sought to exclude undocumented immigrants from the population counts used to calculate the decennial congressional apportionment. The brief argues that the Constitution requires all people, regardless of citizenship or immigration status, to be counted in the census and included in the apportionment base. The amici support this claim by providing the historical context for the framers’ crafting of the Apportionment and Enumeration Clauses, along with discussions of the 14th Amendment, the Reapportionment and Census Act of 1929, and census practice over the centuries. They emphasize that the census was created and has historically served as “a measure of population, not political membership.”
title: Trump v. New York (2020)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Historians of the Census in Support of Appellees
tags: Census, Apportionment, Democracy, Citizenship, 14th Amendment

description: Three scholars of immigration law filed a brief in United States v. Palomar-Santiago, a case that considered the statutory prerequisites for a federal court to dismiss a removal order. The brief explains that the federal statute at issue originated in a racist intent to exclude Mexican immigrants from the United States, and that Congress failed to address that intent when it reenacted the statute in the 1950s. The amici urge the Court to construe the statute’s ambiguities in ways that favor defendants seeking to challenge their deportation as a way of ameliorating the statute’s discriminatory effects.
title: United States v. Palomar-Santiago (2021)
brief_title: Brief for Professors Kelly Lytle Hernández, Mae Ngai, and Ingrid Eagly as Amici Curiae Supporting Respondent
tags: Immigration

description: Eight immigration law and history scholars filed a brief in Department of State v. Muñoz, which ruled, among other things, that an American citizen does not have a constitutionally protected right to bring a noncitizen spouse to the United States. The brief examines historical immigration policies to illustrate the nation’s long-standing commitment and deeply rooted interest in family reunification. The amici explain that even in times of significant immigration restrictions, immigration policies made exceptions and granted special accommodations for immediate family members.
title: United States Department of State v. Muñoz (2024)
brief_title: Brief of Immigration Law and History Scholars as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: Immigration, Citizenship

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Trump v. CASA, a case that raised questions about the legality of nationwide injunctions barring the Trump administration’s executive order rescinding birthright citizenship. Six legal historians with expertise in the history of equity filed a brief supporting the injunctions as traditional equitable remedies. The brief maintains that courts of equity historically granted injunctions that protected both parties and non-parties to a case, as well as injunctions that had very broad scopes. The amici provide historical context to help explain the relative lack of nationwide injunctions prior to the 20th century, pointing to changes in sovereign immunity, jurisdiction, and venue that eliminated legal and practical hurdles to those injunctions. Three legal historians and scholars of immigration law and history filed a brief in support of nationwide injunctions and in opposition to the executive order. The brief explains that the order threatened to disproportionately affect Asian Americans and reverse “a century’s worth of efforts” to ensure equality for Asian Americans. Among other things, the amici highlight the importance of constitutional birthright citizenship guarantees for Asian Americans facing exclusionary immigration and naturalization policies that denied them pathways to naturalization throughout the 19th and 20th centuries.
title: Trump v. CASA, Inc. (2025)
brief_title: Brief of Legal Historians as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents | Brief for Professors Gabriel J. Chin, Erika Lee, and Paul Finkelman as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: Citizenship, 14th Amendment, Citizenship Clause, Nationwide Preliminary Injunctions

description: Four constitutional law and history professors filed a brief in Williams v. Taylor, a case that considered, among other things, whether a state court’s refusal to set aside a criminal defendant’s death sentence was contrary to federal law or rested on an unreasonable application of it. Writing in support of the defendant, the amici argue that the Supreme Court should not defer to the state court’s interpretation of federal law in deciding whether the defendant was eligible for relief under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996. The brief explains that such deference would undermine the framers’ intent in drafting Article III of the Constitution: to empower the federal judiciary to ensure that state courts faithfully follow federal law. Motion for Leave to File Brief Amici Curiae and Brief Amici Curiae of Professors Lance G. Banning, Jack N. Rakove, William W. Van Alstyne, and Gordon G. Young in Support of Petitioner
title: Williams v. Taylor (2000)
tags: Article III, Habeas Corpus

description: Twenty-one legal historians with expertise in English legal history and the founding era filed a brief in Immigration and Naturalization Service v. St. Cyr, a case that upheld, among other things, a deportable noncitizen’s right to habeas corpus in the face of amendments to the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952. The brief looks to both English common law and early American law to demonstrate that habeas corpus has traditionally been available to citizens and noncitizens alike to challenge their unlawful civil or criminal confinement at the hands of the government. According to the amici, these overlapping histories further demonstrate that habeas is a proper vehicle for resolving challenges that hinge on matters of statutory interpretation.
title: Immigration and Naturalization Service v. St. Cyr (2001)
brief_title: Brief Amici Curiae of Legal Historians Listed Herein in Support of Respondent
tags: Habeas Corpus, Citizenship, Immigration

description: Twenty-four legal historians with expertise in English common law and early American legal history filed a brief in Rasul v. Bush, which ruled that people detained at Guantánamo Bay had a right to habeas corpus and could challenge their detentions as unconstitutional. Written to support the availability of habeas to the detainees, the brief shows that the common law writ of habeas corpus was available throughout the territories of the British Empire — even to alleged “enemy aliens” — in the years leading up to the Constitutional Convention. The amici explain that the framers incorporated these common law concepts into the Constitution’s Suspension Clause, and that early American courts routinely upheld them.
title: Rasul v. Bush (2004)
brief_title: Brief Amici Curiae of Legal Historians Listed Herein in Support of the Petitioners
tags: Habeas Corpus, Suspension Clause

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Boumediene v. Bush, a case that, among other things, ruled the Military Commissions Act of 2006 unconstitutional and upheld Guantánamo Bay detainees’ right to habeas corpus. Twenty-five historians with expertise in English common law and early American legal history filed a brief in support of the detainees. The brief reviews the common law history to demonstrate that the writ of habeas corpus was available to detainees regardless of their nationality; that it applied regardless of the “formal sovereign status” of the territory where the detainees were being held; and that it required courts to rigorously and independently review the facts to ensure that detentions were not illegal. Seventeen historians and scholars of the Constitution also filed a brief in support of the detainees. The brief explains that the framers recognized habeas corpus as a crucial bulwark against legislative and executive abuses. The amici argue that the framers intended the habeas guarantee to be judicially enforceable and not subject to statutory override by Congress — a conclusion backed by a long tradition of Supreme Court case law.
title: Boumediene v. Bush (2008)
brief_title: Brief of Legal Historians as Amici Curiae in Support of Petitioners | Brief of Amicus Curiae in Support of Petitioners
tags: Habeas Corpus, Suspension Clause

description: Twenty-three legal historians with expertise in English and early American legal history filed a brief in Department of Homeland Security v. Thuraissigiam, which ruled that a federal statute limiting habeas protections for noncitizens subject to expedited removal did not violate the Constitution’s Suspension or Due Process Clauses. Writing in support of a man facing deportation, the amici draw on English and American legal history to demonstrate the breadth of the people and situations to which habeas protections traditionally applied. They further argue that the framers would not have empowered the federal government to override the writ simply for practical purposes or political expediency.
title: Department of Homeland Security v. Thuraissigiam (2020)
brief_title: Brief of Legal Historians as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondent
tags: Habeas Corpus, Citizenship, Suspension Clause, Due Process Clause

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in District of Columbia v. Heller, which ruled that the Second Amendment guarantees an individual right to bear arms for the purpose of self-defense. Fifteen historians of the founding era and early American legal history filed a brief explaining that the framers did not enshrine a personal right to bear arms in the Second Amendment. The brief explores the original meaning of the amendment through a contextual analysis of British law and founding era constitutional debates. The amici show, among other things, that the question of an individual right to bear arms “never crossed the threshold of constitutional significance in 1787–1789”; instead, they argue, Second Amendment debates centered on the role of militias — thus making the amendment’s preamble critical to understanding the content of its guarantees. The CATO Institute and a historian of Anglo-American legal history filed a brief arguing that English common law granted an individual right to bear arms, especially for self-defense, and that the Second Amendment constitutionalized that right. When translated into the American legal context, the amici explain, the right broadened to recognize the importance of facilitating citizen militias, but it remained at its core a personal right for the purposes of defending one’s home and family.
title: District of Columbia v. Heller (2008)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Jack N. Rakove, Saul Cornell, David T. Konig, William J. Novak, Lois G. Schwoerer et al. in Support of Petitioners | Brief of the CATO Institute and History Professor Joyce Lee Malcolm as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondent
tags: Second Amendment

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in McDonald v. City of Chicago, which held that the individual right to bear arms for self-defense is applicable to the states (and municipalities) under the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause. Thirty-four historians of law, constitutional history, the Second Amendment, and the Reconstruction Amendments filed a brief in support of the local firearms ordinances at issue in the case. The brief argues that states’ and municipalities’ powers to regulate firearms are part of a history and tradition of regulation dating to the antebellum period. The amici demonstrate that after the 14th Amendment was passed, states continued to enact “reasonable non-discriminatory safety regulations, including regulations banning classes of dangerous weapons.” Four historians of early American legal and constitutional history and Pennsylvania history filed a brief in support of the constitutionality of the ordinances. The brief argues that the right to keep and bear arms was the “dominant” motivation for the Second Amendment, and, in turn, that any “right of individual self-defense” recognized at the time of the framing “provided no motivation” for the Second Amendment’s adoption. Six historians and legal scholars of the 14th Amendment filed a brief to challenge the incorporation of the entirety of the Bill of Rights — including the Second Amendment — against the states. The brief argues that incorporation of this kind would upend 135 years of precedent and the distribution of powers between state and federal governments. The amici further contend that neither the 14th Amendment’s plain text, nor its legislative intent or original public meaning, support the incorporation of the Bill of Rights in total — or the Second Amendment alone — against the states. Twenty-one historians of English and early American history filed a brief in support of the local ordinances. The brief asked the Court to reconsider its prior factual findings in District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), arguing that an individual’s right to bear arms for that individual’s “self-defense” was not “deeply rooted in our nation’s traditions.” The amici explain that the right to “have arms” found in the English Declaration of Rights — which formed the basis of the Second Amendment right — “referred to a right to possess arms in defense of the realm.” The brief asserts that the founders shared this understanding, and that the Second Amendment was drafted to reflect as much.
title: McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010)
