tags: Second Amendment, 14th Amendment, Due Process Clause

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, which declared that a New York state law governing licenses for the concealed carry of firearms violated the Second Amendment. Seventeen professors of history and law filed a brief in support of the New York law. The brief emphasizes that both English and American law had, for centuries, restricted the public carry of dangerous weapons to ensure order and peace, and that both sanctioned discretionary licensing regimes. To substantiate that point, the amici survey English and American legal sources from the 13th century through the 20th. Four experts in the fields of linguistics, law, and legal history filed a brief in support of the New York law. The brief uses a corpus linguistics approach to analyze the meaning of the Second Amendment to founding era voters. According to the amici, this approach suggests that ordinary citizens understood that the Second Amendment’s reference to a right to “keep and bear arms” had “a collective, militaristic meaning at the Founding,” and also that the government could regulate that right. The brief emphasizes that advances in corpus linguistics provide judges and lawyers with access to substantially more historical material than was available at the time the Supreme Court decided District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) and McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010).
title: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association, Inc. v. Bruen (2022)
brief_title: Brief for Amici Curiae Professors of History and Law in Support of Respondents | Brief for Corpus Linguistics Professors and Experts as Amici Curiae Supporting Respondents
tags: Second Amendment

description: Eighteen historians and scholars of English and American history and law filed a brief in United States v. Rahimi, a case that upheld a federal law barring individuals under domestic violence restraining orders from possessing firearms. The brief, which supports the law’s constitutionality, documents the long-standing history and tradition of restricting “dangerous” individuals from possessing firearms, beginning with English common law and stretching into the 20th century. It also explains how domestic violence was regulated “to protect the public peace” during the founding era. To support their assertions, the amici draw on published primary and secondary scholarship as well as unpublished primary sources that provide insight into English common law and founding era local customs.
title: United States v. Rahimi (2024)
brief_title: Brief for Amici Curiae Professors of History and Law in Support of Petitioner
tags: Second Amendment

description: Seven historians and legal scholars of Native American law and legal history filed a brief in Dollar General Corp. v. Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians, a case that considered whether tribal courts had jurisdiction in civil tort suits against non–tribe members. The brief argues that tribal jurisdiction over nonmembers’ activities on tribal land — and over civil disputes arising from those activities — extends from tribes’ historical inherent sovereignty. According to the amici, the historical record demonstrates that this jurisdiction has been recognized for centuries, beginning with the first treaties ever signed between a Native American tribe and the United States, and that the federal government has upheld this principle throughout the nation’s subsequent history.
title: Dollar General Corp. v. Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians (2016)
brief_title: Brief for Amici Curiae Historians and Legal Scholars Gregory Ablavsky, Bethany R. Berger, Ned Blackhawk, Daniel Carpenter, Matthew L. M. Fletcher, Maggie McKinley, and Joseph William Singer in Support of Respondents
tags: Federal Indian Law

description: Nine historians and legal scholars with expertise in Oklahoma history and Native American policy joined with the Cherokee Nation to file a brief in McGirt v. Oklahoma, a case that considered whether, under the Major Crimes Act, land reserved for the Creek Nation remained “Indian country” for purposes of determining federal jurisdiction for a crime committed by a tribal member on tribal land. The brief argues that the Creek Nation remains an established tribal authority. The amici explain that although various attempts were made during the 19th and 20th centuries to disestablish the Creek Nation — through settler invasion, removal policy, and assimilation policy, among other policies — these policies failed, and the Creek Nation retains the “same governmental authority as other tribes nationwide.”
title: McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Historians, Legal Scholars, and Cherokee Nation in Support of Petitioner
tags: Federal Indian Law

description: Ten historians and legal scholars of Oklahoma history and Native American law and policy joined with the Cherokee Nation to file a brief in Sharp v. Murphy, a case that considered whether, under the Major Crimes Act, land reserved for the Creek Nation remained “Indian country” for purposes of determining federal jurisdiction for a crime committed by a tribal member on tribal land. The brief argues that the contested land has the same jurisdictional status as Indian lands elsewhere and was never disestablished, notwithstanding the conduct of the federal government and Oklahoma toward the Creek Nation over the course of the 19th and 20th centuries. The amici trace the history of the Creek Nation from the 1830s onward to show, among other things, that state prosecutions of crimes that occurred on the reservation were carried out in defiance of federal law and state and federal precedents.
title: Sharp v. Murphy (2020)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Historians, Legal Scholars, and Cherokee Nation in Support of Respondent
tags: Federal Indian Law

description: Three scholars of federal Indian law and history filed a brief in Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, a case that considered whether both states and the federal government have the power to prosecute non–Native American individuals for crimes they commit against Native people on Native land. The brief argues that only the federal government can prosecute crimes of this type, in keeping with more than 200 years of law and practice. The amici trace this principle from the Constitution through 21st-century congressional legislation. The brief emphasizes that any state jurisdiction over crimes by or against Native people on Native land “is a matter of federal legislative grace.”
title: Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta (2022)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Federal Indian Law Scholars and Historians in Support of Respondent
tags: Federal Indian Law

description: Five scholars who specialize in the history of relations between Native American nations and the United States filed a brief in Arizona v. Navajo Nation, which ruled that the federal government’s failure to assert Colorado River water rights for the Navajo Tribe did not violate the government’s legal duties to the tribe. The brief argues that the federal government failed to fulfill the trust doctrine, an early American agreement between Native American tribes and the federal government that has defined the relationship throughout the country’s history. Among other things, the amici describe how Congress and the executive branch have bound themselves since the founding era to protect and care for Native American nations, including by ensuring that they have adequate water for their homelands.
title: Arizona v. Navajo Nation (2023)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Historians in Support of Respondents
tags: Federal Indian Law

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Haaland v. Brackeen, a case that upheld the constitutionality of the Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (ICWA). The American Historical Association and the Organization of American Historians filed a brief in support of ICWA’s constitutionality. The amici situate ICWA in a history and tradition of federal regulation of Native children and families dating back to the founding era and stretching into the 20th century, arguing that, in that respect, the statute falls within Congress’s constitutional powers. The brief further shows how ICWA sought to correct failed federal policies — including those that encouraged state governments to separate large numbers of Native children from their families and their nations — by strengthening tribal jurisdiction and establishing protections against future abuses by the states. A legal scholar and historian of federal Indian law also filed a brief supporting ICWA’s constitutionality. The brief looks to the Constitution’s text and to early American history and practice to demonstrate the constitutionality of Congress’s attempts to regulate Native American affairs, especially on matters of child welfare. The amici also challenge narrower accounts of federal power over Native affairs, showing how those accounts resemble arguments lodged by state advocates and rejected by courts over the course of several centuries.
title: Haaland v. Brackeen (2023)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae American Historical Association and Organization of American Historians in Support of Federal and Tribal Parties | Brief of Amicus Curiae Professor Gregory Ablavsky in Support of Federal Parties and Tribal Defendants
tags: Federal Indian Law

description: Four historians of early American constitutional history and political representation filed a brief in Vieth v. Jubelirer, a case that left open the question of partisan gerrymandering’s constitutionality. The brief argues that partisan gerrymandering contradicts the founding era principle of fair representation that underpinned the framers’ design of Article I of the Constitution. As the amici explain, the framers believed that politicians should not be able to manipulate the composition of the House of Representatives and sought to ensure that the House “mirrored” the composition of the community it represented. According to the brief, redistricting practices that allow parties to create safe seats for themselves or to convert a minority of votes into a supermajority of seats are therefore unconstitutional.
title: Vieth v. Jubelirer (2004)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Jack N. Rakove, Alexander Keyssar, Peter S. Onuf and Rosemarie Zagarri in Support of Appellants
tags: Partisan Gerrymandering, Elections, Democracy, Article I

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Arizona State Legislature v. Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission, a case that upheld the constitutionality of Arizona’s independent redistricting commission drawing the state’s congressional districts. Five historians with expertise in colonial and founding era history filed a brief in support of the commission. The brief explains, among other things, that the ballot initiative process through which Arizona voters created the commission was consistent with founding era ideas of popular sovereignty and the legislative power of the people as distinct from their legislators. Three scholars and historians of Congressional redistricting also filed a brief in support of the commission. The brief argues that the Court should have resolved the case on statutory rather than constitutional grounds. The amici include a detailed discussion of the legislative history of the statute now codified at 2 U.S.C. § 2a(c), arguing that Congress enacted it to empower states to redistrict according to their own specific lawmaking procedures. In doing so, the brief explains, Congress was lawfully exercising its power under the Constitution’s Elections Clause to set the rules for federal elections.
title: Arizona State Legislature v. Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission (2015)
brief_title: Brief of Jack N. Rakove, Richard R. Beeman, Alexander Keyssar, Peter S. Onuf, and Rosemarie Zagarri as Amici Curiae in Support of Appellees | Brief of Scholars and Historians of Congressional Redistricting as Amici Curiae in Support of Appellees
tags: Redistricting, Elections, Democracy

description: Thirty historians and scholars of the Voting Rights Act (VRA) and the civil rights era filed a brief in Shelby County v. Holder, a case in which the Supreme Court invalidated the formula used to determine the jurisdictions covered by Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. The brief argues, among other things, that Congress acted consistently with the VRA’s original purposes when, in 2006, it reauthorized the VRA with a focus on “second-generation tactics” that discriminated against minority voters in ways beyond denying those voters access to the ballot box. The amici assert that the VRA’s most recent coverage formula was as precise as any that the Court previously upheld.
title: Shelby County v. Holder (2013)
brief_title: Brief of Historians and Social Scientists as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: Voting Rights Act, Elections, Democracy, 14th Amendment, 15th Amendment, 10th Amendment, Article IV

description: Fifteen scholars of American history filed a brief in Gill v. Whitford, a case that considered the constitutionality of partisan gerrymandering. The brief argues that the founding ideal of representative democracy requires a close correspondence between the public and their elected officials, and that partisan gerrymandering severs that correspondence by entrenching officials’ power and undermining their political accountability. The amici explain that the 1st and 14th Amendments both reflect that vision of representative democracy and protect rights necessary to sustain it. They also document that partisan gerrymandering has been denounced as unconstitutional and antidemocratic throughout American history.
title: Gill v. Whitford (2018)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Historians in Support of Appellees
tags: Partisan Gerrymandering, Redistricting, Elections, Democracy, First Amendment, 14th Amendment

description: Ten historians with expertise in voting rights and U.S. elections filed a brief in Husted v. A. Philip Randolph Institute, in which the Supreme Court declared that Ohio’s practice of canceling the registrations of nonvoters did not violate the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 (NVRA). The brief argues that Ohio’s procedure is illegal. It explains that states began purging nonvoters in the early 20th century to maintain accurate voter registration lists, but that over time, both the states and Congress came to see this practice as ineffective and unfair, potentially contributing to low turnout and disproportionately burdening lower-income and minority voters. The amici further show that Congress enacted the NVRA’s prohibition of removal “by reason of the person’s failure to vote” to encourage states to use more precise and less discriminatory methods for identifying ineligible voters, and that the Department of Justice acted with this understanding until recently.
title: Husted v. A. Philip Randolph Institute (2018)
brief_title: Brief for American History Professors as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: Elections, Democracy, Voting Rights, National Voter Registration Act

description: Sixteen founding era historians filed a brief in Rucho v. Common Cause and Lamone v. Benisek, two cases that considered the constitutionality of partisan gerrymandering. The brief argues that partisan gerrymandering is antithetical to the founding era principle of fair and effective representation. As the amici explain, the 1st and 14th Amendments and Article I of the Constitution reflect founding era concerns that legislators would entrench their power by manipulating election rules and stifling political expression. Likewise, the brief shows, the framers empowered the federal judiciary to counter legislative overreach. The amici contend that voters should therefore have effective judicial remedies against partisan gerrymandering. They underscore that the constitutional question in these cases did not turn on the Constitution’s text but rather on “fundamental substantive founding principles,” founding era debates, and other sources.
title: Rucho v. Common Cause (2019); Lamone v. Benisek (2019)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Historians in Support of Appellees
tags: Partisan Gerrymandering, Redistricting, Elections, Democracy, First Amendment, 14th Amendment, Article I, Article III

description: Ten scholars of Alabama history filed a brief in Allen v. Milligan, which ruled that Alabama’s 2021 congressional redistricting plan likely violated Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act. The brief explains that Alabama’s “Black Belt region” — a majority-Black part of the state — is a “community of interest” that should be prioritized when the state’s electoral districts are drawn. To illustrate that residents of the Black Belt have a shared history going back two centuries, the amici document the region’s roots in slavery and describe the economic hardship, exclusion from social services, and other discrimination that Black Belt residents have historically faced.
title: Allen v. Milligan (2023)
brief_title: Brief for Alabama Historians as Amici Curiae Supporting Appellee-Respondents
tags: Redistricting, Elections, Democracy, Voting Rights Act

description: Thirty historians and legal scholars of the American South filed a brief in Alexander v. South Carolina State Conference of the NAACP, a case that rejected a racial gerrymandering challenge to South Carolina’s congressional map. Supporting the conclusion that the map racially discriminated against Black voters, the brief surveys the long history of racial discrimination in South Carolina politics aimed at diminishing the power of Black voters. The amici also position the 2020 round of congressional redistricting as the latest instance in a recurring pattern of discrimination against Black voters dating back to Reconstruction.
title: Alexander v. South Carolina State Conference of the NAACP (2024)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Historians in Support of Appellees and Affirmance
tags: Racial Gerrymandering, Redistricting, Elections, Democracy

description: Three historians with expertise in the history of Louisiana and the American South filed a brief in Louisiana v. Callais and Robinson v. Callais, two cases that considered whether a remedial congressional map for Louisiana was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander. In supporting the creation of a second majority-Black congressional district, the brief argues that the district encompassed a well-established community of interest united by a shared history and common needs, including a common lineage of slavery. The amici further show that the residents of the district experience hardships stemming from their shared experiences of racial discrimination.
title: Louisiana v. Callais (2025); Robinson v. Callais (2025)
brief_title: Brief for Louisiana Historians as Amici Curiae Supporting Appellants
tags: Racial Gerrymandering, Redistricting, Elections, Democracy, Voting Rights Act

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Locke v. Davey, which ruled that the state of Washington did not violate the First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause by prohibiting funding for devotional theology instruction. Twenty-four historians and legal scholars of religion and the First Amendment filed a brief supporting the state. The brief challenges the argument that the Washington Constitution’s ban on funding reflected anti-Catholic or nativist sentiment. Instead, the amici explain, that constitution’s no-funding principle was based on “principles of religious liberty and rights of conscience” and resembles provisions incorporated into many other state constitutions over the course of the 19th century “for reasons unrelated to anti-Catholic animus.” The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, the Catholic League for Religious and Civil Rights, and 18 religious historians and legal scholars filed a brief supporting state funding for religious instruction. Situating the Washington Constitution in a broader trend of 19th-century federal and state laws and policies designed to disfavor Catholic schools in particular, the brief argues that Washington’s no-funding rule is rooted in nativism and hostility toward European immigrants and their religions.
title: Locke v. Davey (2004)
brief_title: Brief Amicus Curiae of Historians and Law Scholars on Behalf of Petitioners Gary Locke, et al. | Brief of Amici Curiae The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, The Catholic League for Religious and Civil Rights, and Historians and Legal Scholars in Support of Respondent
tags: First Amendment, Free Exercise Clause, Religion

description: Forty legal historians and scholars of religion and law filed a brief in Town of Greece v. Galloway, which held that a town’s practice of opening legislative meetings with a prayer does not violate the First Amendment’s Establishment Clause. In opposing the town’s practice, the brief explains that the framers were particularly concerned about religious language in political discourse that could divide rather than unite; that they believed that religious language in public life should be “universal and non-sectarian”; and that they were averse to coerced religious observation. The amici argue that because this town’s prayer exerted substantial pressure on citizens looking to participate in town politics, the framers would not have supported it.
title: Town of Greece v. Galloway (2014)
brief_title: Brief for Paul Finkelman, Steven K. Green, Michael I. Meyerson, John A. Ragosta, and 36 Other Legal Historians and Scholars of Religion and American Law as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: First Amendment, Establishment Clause, Religion

description: Nine historians and scholars of American history filed a brief in Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, which ruled that federal regulations requiring for-profit employers with religious objections to nonetheless provide their employees with health insurance coverage for contraception violated the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993. The brief, in support of neither party to the case, explores the history of corporate treatment under the law and argues that the law has not historically granted for-profit businesses the same liberty interests that “natural persons” (as distinct from artificial entities such as businesses) enjoy.
title: Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc. (2014)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Historians and Legal Scholars Supporting Neither Party
tags: Reproductive Rights, Corporate Law, Affordable Care Act, Religious Freedom Restoration Act, Religion, Free Exercise Clause

description: Seven military historians filed a brief in Zubik v. Burwell, a case that challenged accommodations allowing employers with religious objections to opt out of providing contraceptive coverage to their employees, and to pass that cost on to the government or medical insurance companies. The brief argues that American law has long deployed accommodations like those in question to balance the religious liberty of some with the personal interests of others, and to balance both with “the important interests of the government.” The amici draw parallels between the accommodations at issue and historical conscientious objector laws that required people who objected to military service to pay money or provide alternative service to the country.
title: Zubik v. Burwell (2016)
brief_title: Brief of Military Historians as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: Reproductive Rights, Affordable Care Act, Religious Freedom Restoration Act, Religion, Free Exercise Clause

description: Ten legal and religious historians filed a brief in Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia v. Comer, a case that considered whether the First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause permits churches to be excluded from a secular state aid program. The brief argues that the no-funding principle found in Article I, § 7 of the Missouri Constitution and other state laws “arose independently of anti-religious animus” and actually reflected goals of preventing state support of religion and ensuring the financial security of developing public school systems.
title: Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Inc. v. Comer (2017)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Legal and Religious Historians, in Support of Respondent
tags: First Amendment, Free Exercise Clause, Religion

description: Twenty-two historians and scholars of constitutional history and religious freedom filed a brief in American Legion v. American Humanist Association, a case that considered the constitutionality of a Maryland town’s display and maintenance of a Latin cross. The brief explains that the framers considered the new nation to be religiously pluralist and sought to ensure that government speech was universal and nonsectarian insofar as it referenced religion. The cross, the amici conclude, violated those commitments. In addition, they urge the Court to recognize that the Establishment Clause sought not only to prevent government coercion but also to avoid government action that could provoke animosity or division among people of different faiths.
title: American Legion v. American Humanist Association (2019)
brief_title: Brief for Historians and Legal Scholars as Amici Curiae Supporting Respondents
tags: First Amendment, Establishment Clause

description: Five historians of American military history filed a brief in Little Sisters of the Poor Saints Peter and Paul Home v. Pennsylvania, a case that upheld the federal government’s authority to exempt employers with religious and moral objections from the Affordable Care Act’s requirement to provide contraceptive coverage to employees. The brief — like one filed in Zubik v. Burwell (2016) — argues that American law has long deployed accommodations to balance the religious liberty of some with the personal interests of others, and to balance both with “the important interests of the government.” As in the Zubik brief, the amici draw parallels between the accommodations at issue and historical conscientious objector laws that required people who objected to military service to pay money or provide alternative service to the country.
title: Little Sisters of the Poor Saints Peter and Paul Home v. Pennsylvania (2020)
brief_title: Brief of Military Historians as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: Reproductive Rights, Affordable Care Act, Religious Freedom Restoration Act, Religion, Free Exercise Clause

description: Thirteen legal historians filed a brief in Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta, which ruled that a California regulation requiring charitable organizations to disclose donors’ details to the state’s attorney general violated the First Amendment. The brief urges the Court to account for the specific historical circumstances that informed its defense of associational rights when, in NAACP v. Alabama (1958), it weighed how to balance donors’ privacy interests with the state’s interest in detecting fraud. As the amici explain, the “dire circumstances” that called for shielding the NAACP’s donors from disclosure in the 1950s — namely, government-sponsored public and private violence against Black people — were not in play in present-day California.
title: Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta (2021)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Legal Historians in Support of Respondent
tags: First Amendment, Freedom of Association

description: Seven scholars of history, journalism, and the First Amendment’s Free Press Clause filed a brief in Moody v. NetChoice and NetChoice v. Paxton, two cases involving constitutional challenges to state laws attempting to regulate social media websites’ content moderation policies. The brief, which supports the websites’ claims to have First Amendment rights to editorial discretion, examines the history of printers and press freedom. The amici explain that social media sites’ discretion to determine what content to distribute today is analogous to the constitutionally protected discretion to publish enjoyed by printers, the press, and others during the founding era.
title: Moody v. NetChoice, LLC (2024); NetChoice, LLC v. Paxton (2024)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Professors of History in Support of Respondents in No. 22-277 and Petitioners in No. 22-555
tags: First Amendment, Social Media, Free Speech Clause, Free Press Clause

description: Eighteen scholars of the First Amendment filed a brief in Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton, a case that considered the constitutionality of a Texas law mandating age verification methods for pornography websites. The brief argues that laws restricting children’s access to pornography are consistent with the framers’ understanding of the First Amendment. The amici maintain that the framers were “not free-speech absolutists” and recognized the role of the state in barring access to obscene materials. Amicus Curiae Brief of Scholars in Support of Respondent
title: Free Speech Coalition, Inc. v. Paxton (2025)
tags: First Amendment, Free Speech Clause

description: Eighteen historians and legal scholars with expertise in constitutional history and the First Amendment filed a brief in Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board v. Drummond, a case that considered, among other things, whether the Free Exercise Clause requires a state to provide financial support to religious schools when it also provides financial support to nongovernmental secular entities that operate schools. The brief argues that state and local governments are not required to provide public funding under the Free Exercise Clause. The amici present federal and state funding practices from the founding era through the early 19th century to demonstrate that “the free-exercise principle was not originally understood to include the right to public funding of religious schools.”
title: Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board v. Drummond (2025)
brief_title: Brief of Historians and Legal Scholars as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondent
tags: First Amendment, Free Exercise Clause, Establishment Clause, Religion

description: A scholar of American history and law filed a brief in Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy, which ruled that the Seventh Amendment entitles defendants to a jury trial when the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) seeks civil penalties. In supporting the constitutionality of the statutory provisions shielding the SEC’s administrative law judges from removal by the president, the brief explains that the original understanding of the president’s removal power was not unfettered. Rather, the amici argue, the history of pre-founding England and the early United States reveals that insulating executive officials (like the SEC’s judges) from removal was consistent with the understanding of executive power enshrined in the Constitution.
title: Securities and Exchange Commission v. Jarkesy (2024)
brief_title: Brief of Amicus Curiae Professor Jed H. Shugerman in Support of Petitioner
tags: Administrative Law, Democracy

description: Six scholars of constitutional law and early American history filed a brief in Consumer Financial Protection Bureau v. Community Financial Services Association of America, a case that verified the constitutionality of the funding scheme that Congress established for the bureau. The brief, which supports the funding scheme, explains that the Constitution’s Appropriations Clause gives Congress alone the power to decide how federal agencies are funded. Drawing on the history of legislative appropriations beginning in England several centuries before the American Revolution and continuing through the 19th century, the amici conclude that Congress was exercising its constitutionally conferred authority when it designed the bureau’s funding mechanism.
title: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau v. Community Financial Services Association of America, Ltd. (2024)
brief_title: Brief of Professors of History and Constitutional Law as Amici Curiae in Support of Petitioners
tags: Administrative Law, Appropriations Clause, Congressional Power, Federal Agencies, Independent Agencies

description: Three legal historians filed a brief in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Relentless v. Department of Commerce, the cases in which the Supreme Court overturned Chevron deference. The brief, which supports Chevron’s constitutionality, describes a long history of federal courts deferring to federal agencies’ decision-making that began in the founding era and continued through the 20th century. It also shows that court deference to federal agencies’ legal interpretations is consistent with the founding generation’s understanding of the separation of powers.
title: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024); Relentless, Inc. v. Department of Commerce (2024)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Historians Gautham Rao, Richard R. John, and Jane Manners in Support of Respondents
tags: Chevron Doctrine, Administrative Law, Democracy

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Kiobel v. Royal Dutch Petroleum, a case that considered whether, under the Alien Tort Statute (ATS), corporations are immune from liability for violating the laws of nations, and whether U.S. courts have authority to hear cases based on such violations committed outside the United States. The case was reargued, leading to a second round of amicus briefing. Nine legal historians filed a brief in support of corporate tort liability under the ATS for violations of international law. The brief argues that a corporate exemption from liability would be “inconsistent with the text, history, and purpose” of the ATS, which the First Congress designed to ensure remedies for just such violations. The amici examine tort suits against English and early American corporations to substantiate their claims. Eighteen scholars of international trials and Nuremberg era jurisprudence filed a brief in support of corporate liability under the ATS. The brief argues that Nuremberg era jurisprudence supports holding corporations accountable for violations of customary international law. In particular, the amici explain how the Allied Control Council sanctioned corporations outside the courts through measures like dissolution, asset seizure, and reparations. Six scholars with expertise in the Nuremberg trials and post–World War II legal practice filed a brief taking no position in the ultimate dispute and focusing instead on arguments raised by other amicus filings. The amici argue that the Nuremberg trials did not establish an “international norm of corporate criminal liability” that could support contemporary ATS claims. Among other things, the brief contends that no corporations were charged or served as defendants in the trials, and it explores the difficulties associated with drawing consistent legal principles from the conduct of the Allies toward German business corporations in the postwar period. Five legal historians with expertise in the ATS filed a brief to support corporate tort liability under the ATS for violations of international law. The brief argues that the original text, history, and purpose of the ATS show that it offers plaintiffs recourse to the federal courts to address violations of the law of nations, including torts committed by corporations. The amici explain, among other things, that Congress did not restrict the kinds of defendants that plaintiffs could sue, and that it used domestic common law principles to adjudicate claims against corporations for violating the law of nations. Two legal historians with expertise in the ATS filed a brief arguing that the federal courts have jurisdiction to rule on ATS claims for torts that violate international law, regardless of the citizenship of the defendants. The amici support their assertions through an examination of the text and drafting history of the ATS, early understandings of Article III of the Constitution, and 18th-century case law.
title: Kiobel v. Royal Dutch Petroleum Co. (2013)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Professors of Legal History Barbara Aronstein Black, William R. Casto, Martin S. Flaherty, Robert W. Gordon, Nasser Hussain, Stanley N. Katz, Michael Lobban, John V. Orth, and Anne-Marie Slaughter in Support of Petitioners | Brief of Amici Curiae Nuremberg Scholars Omer Bartov, Michael J. Bazyler, Donald Bloxham, Lawrence Douglas, Hilary Earl, Hon. Bruce J. Einhorn, Ret., David Fraser, Sam Garkawe, Stanley A. Goldman, Gregory S. Gordon, Kevin Jon Heller, Michael J. Kelly, Matthew Lippman, Michael Marrus, Fionnuala D. Ní Aoláin, Kim Chistian Priemel, Christoph Safferling and Frederick Taylor in Support of Petitioners | Brief Amici Curiae of Nuremberg Historians and International Lawyers in Support of Neither Party | Brief of Amici Curiae Professors of Legal History William R. Casto, Martin S. Flaherty, Robert W. Gordon, Nasser Hussain, and John V. Orth in Support of Petitioners | Brief on Reargument of Professors of Legal History and Federal Jurisdiction, Martin S. Flaherty and John V. Orth, as Amici Curiae in Support of Petitioners
tags: Corporate Law, Tort Law, International Law, Alien Tort Statute

description: Five legal historians with expertise in the Alien Tort Statute (ATS) filed a brief in Jesner v. Arab Bank, which ruled that the ATS does not allow lawsuits against corporations. The brief argues that the statute’s text, history, and purpose allow for corporate liability. The brief explains that the founders understood that “corporate liability . . . would be resolved based on common-law principles.” It also analyzes historical case law to demonstrate courts’ long-standing recognition of corporate liability for the torts of corporate agents — a practice that was evident in English courts’ handling of cases against corporations in the 18th century, and that continued into 19th-century America with the rise of modern corporations.
title: Jesner v. Arab Bank, PLC (2018)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Professors of Legal History William R. Casto, Martin S. Flaherty, Stanley N. Katz, Samuel Moyn, and Anne-Marie Slaughter in Support of Petitioners
tags: Corporate Law, Tort Law, International Law, Alien Tort Statute

description: Nine legal historians filed a brief in Nestlé USA v. Doe, a case that considered whether certain domestic corporations could be held liable under the Alien Tort Statute (ATS). The brief argues that recognizing tort liability for domestic corporations aligns with the statute’s history, text, and purpose. It presents records from the First Congress, the first Washington administration, and other founding era legal sources to establish that the ATS was passed and implemented to address “law of nations violations in situations that involved U.S. subjects or territory.”
title: Nestlé USA, Inc. v. Doe (2021)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Professors of Legal History Barbara Aronstein Black, Nikolas Bowie, William R. Casto, Martin S. Flaherty, David Golove, Eliga H. Gould, Stanley N. Katz, Samuel Moyn, and Anne-Marie Slaughter in Support of Respondents
tags: Corporate Law, Tort Law, International Law, Alien Tort Statute

description: Eight historians of the Holocaust and the Nuremberg trials filed a brief in Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp, which ruled that the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act’s expropriation exception incorporates the “domestic takings” rule, and that Germany did not violate international law when its Nazi government coerced German Jewish art dealers to sell a collection of medieval relics. The brief, filed in support of neither party to the case, sought to provide historical context necessary to understand how the Holocaust affected the treatment of German Jewish businesspeople in the period when the relics were sold. Among other things, the amici explain that the Nazis’ comprehensive persecution of Jewish people began with Hitler’s ascension to power in 1933. They also document how the Nazis targeted the social, political, and economic rights of Jewish people with restrictions on employment, education, marriage, and more through 1935.
title: Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp (2021)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Holocaust and Nuremberg Historians in Support of Neither Party
tags: Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act; International Law

description: Eighteen historians and law professors who specialize in 19th-century U.S. history filed a brief in Students for Fair Admissions v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, a case that declared race-conscious college admissions policies unconstitutional. The brief, filed in defense of affirmative action, explains that the Reconstruction Congress designed the 14th Amendment to further racial equality, and that it in fact embraced a variety of race-conscious efforts to achieve that goal. Consequently, the amici argue, the 14th Amendment would not prohibit race-conscious admissions policies.
title: Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College (2023)
brief_title: Brief of Professors of History and Law as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: Affirmative Action, 14th Amendment, Equal Protection Clause

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Parents Involved in Community Schools v. Seattle School District No. 1, which ruled that several public school districts’ approaches to considering race in their student assignment processes violated the 14th Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause. Sixty historians of Reconstruction and the civil rights era filed a brief in support of the schools’ assignment policies. The brief argues that the school district’s policies align with the 14th Amendment’s original purpose and intent, as well as the amendment’s early implementation. The amici contend that the Reconstruction Amendments’ primary goal was to “incorporate[e] Blacks into the civic, economic, and political mainstream of American society”; they explain that race-conscious programs were established at the national and local levels to accomplish this goal. In particular, they emphasize that the Reconstruction Congress approved of and funded a series of race-conscious programs to integrate schools. Eight historians and legal scholars of the civil rights era also filed a brief in support of the schools’ assignment policies. The brief explores these policies as part of the nation’s historical attempts to overcome racial segregation in schools, reflecting the historical role of public schools as “engines of democracy and opportunity.” The amici also emphasize that these kinds of policies represent a democratic consensus achieved over time, and that such policies are “fully consistent with the Court’s education and school desegregation jurisprudence.” The brief explains that there is a long history and tradition of recognizing the autonomy of local schools and deferring to elected officials on matters of educational policy.
title: Parents Involved in Community Schools v. Seattle School District No. 1 (2007)
brief_title: Brief of Historians as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents | Brief of Historians of the Civil Rights Era William H. Chafe, Davison Douglas, Charles Payne, Tomiko Brown-Nagin, Kenneth Mack, Risa Goluboff, Kevin Kruse and Matt Lassiter as Amici Curiae Supporting Respondents
tags: 14th Amendment, Equal Protection Clause, Affirmative Action

description: Seventy-six historians and scholars of the Civil War, Reconstruction, and race and the law filed a brief in Schuette v. Coalition to Defend Affirmative Action, a case that considered the constitutionality of a state constitutional amendment prohibiting race- and sex-based discrimination and preferential treatment in public university admissions. The brief argues that the framers drafted the 14th Amendment to remove special burdens on racial minorities’ ability to seek legislative change. The amici explain that after the Civil War, formerly enslaved Black men and women could not seek legislative change to address continued systemic racial exclusion and violence. The brief also positions both the 14th Amendment and the Civil Rights Act of 1866 as conscious products of a concerted effort to remedy this state of affairs.
title: Schuette v. Coalition to Defend Affirmative Action (2014)
brief_title: Brief of Paul Finkelman and 75 Other Historians and Scholars as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: 14th Amendment, Equal Protection Clause, Affirmative Action

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Hamdan v. Rumsfeld, a case that considered the legality of a special military commission established by the executive branch to try enemy combatants during the war on terror. Three legal historians filed a brief challenging the contention that executive military commissions historically had tried enemy combatants under procedures set solely by the president. The brief looks to the Barbary Wars, an early 19th-century pair of wars that the United States fought with several North African states, to demonstrate that the founding generation followed “recognized international law and custom” in dealing with “unconventional enemies.” Among other things, the amici explain that these customs included “extraordinary deference to standard military detention and adjudication procedures.” Three historians and legal scholars filed a brief challenging the government’s reliance on Ex Parte Quirin (1942) to justify ordering trials by military commission. The brief draws on the historical circumstances surrounding Quirin to condemn it as “an illegitimate precedent that offends this nation’s modern sense of justice.” To support their claim, the amici point, among other things, to judicial bias and conflicts of interest among the Supreme Court justices who issued the ruling. Eight historians of the founding era and early American military history filed a brief opposing the commission and responding to the argument that the founders held an expansive view of executive power that granted the president unilateral power and significant discretion in dealing with military and diplomatic affairs. The brief argues that the founding generation instead sought legislative supervision and control of the executive, in keeping with a deeper Anglo-American rejection of monarchical ideas of executive prerogative. In light of this understanding, the amici assert, the framers divided the powers relating to military and foreign affairs between the president and Congress. Eight scholars of military history and law filed a brief contesting the legality of the commission. The brief argues that the president’s power to create procedures for military commissions are limited by, among other things, the historical understanding of military commissions as invoked in Article 36 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice. To support their assertions, the amici examine the code’s legislative history, beginning with the 1916 Revised Articles of War and subsequent revisions, as well as the history of military commissions prior during the Mexican War, the Civil War, and the military occupation of the Philippines.
title: Hamdan v. Rumsfeld (2006)

description: Twenty-one scholars of American religious history law filed a brief in Trump v. Hawaii, a case that considered the legality of an executive order suspending the entry of foreign nationals into the United States. The brief, filed in support of neither party to the case, focuses on the history of religious discrimination against Mormon immigrants to alert the Court to the importance of strict judicial scrutiny of laws motivated by fears of religious minorities.
title: Trump v. Hawaii (2018)
brief_title: Brief of Scholars of Mormon History and Law as Amici Curiae in Support of Neither Party
tags: Executive Power, Immigration, Religious Discrimination, First Amendment, Establishment Clause

description: Fifteen historians of the founding era filed a brief in Trump v. United States, a case that granted broad new immunities from criminal prosecution to presidents for acts committed while in office. In urging the Court to reject such immunities, the brief explains that presidential immunity contradicts the founding generation’s rejection of monarchical privilege and concerns about abuses of executive power. The amici also argue that attempts by presidents to overturn the results of elections they lost constitute fundamental crimes against the democratic order.
title: Trump v. United States (2024)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Scholars of the Founding Era in Support of Respondent
tags: Presidential Immunity, Executive Power, Democracy

description: Seven historians of the Civil War and Reconstruction filed a brief in Patterson v. McLean Credit Union, a case that examined the applicability of a federal antidiscrimination statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1981, to claims of racial discrimination in the workplace. The brief urges the Court to reaffirm its earlier holding that Section 1981 bars racial discrimination in contracts between private individuals. The amici explain that this reading of the statute aligns with the original intent of the Civil Rights Act of 1866. They also contend that the Reconstruction Congress passed the act “to protect the rights of both blacks and whites, notwithstanding whether the source of a civil rights violation was a private individual, a state official, or a discriminatory state statute or local ordinance.” The brief provides important historical context to understand the act’s purpose, including the patterns of violence and terror that white Southerner inflicted on Black people who attempted to negotiate contracts or enforce their contractual rights.
title: Patterson v. McLean Credit Union (1989)
brief_title: Brief Amicus Curiae of Eric Foner, John H. Franklin, Louis R. Harlan, Stanley N. Katz, Leon F. Litwack, C. Vann Woodward, and Mary Frances Berry
tags: Racial Discrimination, Workplace Discrimination, Civil Rights Law

description: Four legal historians filed a brief in Honda Motor Co. v. Oberg, a case in which the Supreme Court ultimately ruled that the Oregon Constitution’s bar on judicial review of the size of punitive damages awards violated the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause. The brief argues that review of punitive damages awards for excessiveness “is not part of the Anglo-American legal tradition.” The amici base their analysis on a review of English common law, American colonial practice, and 19th-century American legal practice. Among other things, they emphasize that the U.S. Constitution’s original due process guarantees were “adopted . . . against a background assumption that the jury was virtually all-powerful,” and were in keeping with colonial American beliefs that judicial control over juries was tyrannical.
title: Honda Motor Co. v. Oberg (1994)
brief_title: Brief of Legal Historians Daniel R. Coquillette, Mark M. Hager, Bruce H. Mann, and Arthur F. McEvoy as Amici Curiae
tags: Judicial Review, 14th Amendment, Democracy, Due Process

description: Sixty-two scholars with expertise in the history of housing segregation filed a brief in Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, which ruled that disparate impact claims are cognizable under the Fair Housing Act of 1968 (FHA). The brief provides historical context for the federal, state, and local government policies that created racially segregated residential patterns in cities across the country. The amici argue that disparate impact claims ensure that contemporary housing policies will not perpetuate these patterns and should be permitted to advance the FHA’s objective.
title: Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. (2015)
brief_title: Brief of Housing Scholars as Amici Curiae Supporting Respondent
tags: Housing, Racial Discrimination

description: Two scholars of the law and history of the U.S. territories, U.S. sovereignty, and Puerto Rico filed a brief in Puerto Rico v. Sánchez Valle, which ruled that the United States and Puerto Rico are not separate sovereigns for double jeopardy purposes. The brief supports the position that Puerto Rico and the United States are not separate sovereigns, notwithstanding the ratification of Puerto Rico’s Constitution in 1952. The amici explain that there is a long American tradition of distinguishing between autonomy and sovereignty, and that separate sovereignty has historically been tied to statehood. They further contend that neither Congress’s approval of Puerto Rico’s Constitution nor Puerto Rico’s extensive autonomy equate to sovereignty as understood under American law.
title: Puerto Rico v. Sánchez Valle (2016)
brief_title: Brief for Amici Curiae Professors Christina Duffy Ponsa and Sam Erman in Support of Respondents
tags: Fifth Amendment, Double Jeopardy, Sovereignty

description: Six legal historians filed a brief in Hernandez v. Mesa, a case arising from a U.S. Border Patrol agent’s fatal shooting of a Mexican citizen across the U.S.-Mexico border. The brief, filed in support of the Mexican citizen, argues that the Fifth Amendment’s due process protections are not limited to American citizens or inhabitants of the United States. The amici explore the early history of the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, explaining that the framers intended to protect all people from arbitrary governmental action. In addition, the brief emphasizes that the history of the formulation of the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause reaffirms that the “persons” entitled to constitutional due process protections include both citizens and noncitizens.
title: Hernandez v. Mesa (2017)
brief_title: Brief for Amici Curiae Legal Historians in Support of Petitioners
tags: Fourth Amendment, Fifth Amendment, 14th Amendment, Due Process Clause, Qualified Immunity

description: A legal historian with expertise in the history of the Constitution’s Contract Clause filed a brief in Sveen v. Melin, which ruled that the retroactive application of Minnesota’s so-called revocation-upon-divorce statute did not violate the clause. The brief argues that this statute does in fact violate the Contract Clause, both as originally understood in the founding era and as applied throughout the 19th century. The amici encourage the Court to reject its 20th-century Contract Clause jurisprudence and return to the clause’s original meaning.
title: Sveen v. Melin (2018)
brief_title: Brief of Professor James W. Ely, Jr. as Amicus Curiae Supporting Respondent
tags: Contract Clause

description: Twelve scholars of the Fourth Amendment filed a brief in Carpenter v. United States, which ruled that the federal government’s acquisition of cell-site records without a warrant was unconstitutional. The brief analyzes the Fourth Amendment’s text and historical context, arguing, among other things, that such warrantless searches threaten the personal liberty that the framers designed the Fourth Amendment to protect.
title: Carpenter v. United States (2018)
brief_title: Brief of Scholars of the History and Original Meaning of the Fourth Amendment as Amici Curiae in Support of Petitioner
tags: Fourth Amendment, Search and Seizure

description: Four scholars with expertise in the constitutional implications of American territorial expansion filed a brief in Financial Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico v. Aurelius Investment, which ruled that the Constitution’s Appointments Clause does not restrict the appointment of members of the Financial Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico. The brief argues against relying on the Insular Cases — a series of early 20th-century Court opinions regarding the status of U.S. territories acquired in the Spanish-American War — to decide this case. The amici maintain that the Insular Cases do not inform the meaning or scope of the Appointments Clause. They further explain that those cases present constitutional concerns and reflect imperialist and racist thinking that should not be incorporated into contemporary legal doctrine.
title: Financial Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico v. Aurelius Investment, LLC (2020)
brief_title: Brief for Amici Curiae Scholars of Constitutional Law and Legal History Supporting the First Circuit’s Ruling on the Appointments Clause Issue
tags: Appointments Clause

description: Twelve historians of Reconstruction filed a brief in Comcast Corp. v. National Association of African American-Owned Media, which ruled that a plaintiff suing for racial discrimination under the federal civil rights statute 42 U.S.C. § 1981 must prove that race was a but-for cause of the defendant’s actions. The brief argues that Section 1981 is the product of Reconstruction era efforts to dramatically expand the federal government’s authority to guarantee basic civil rights, including eliminating racial discrimination of any kind in contracts. The amici explain that but-for causation undermines the original purpose and meaning of the statute by allowing defendants to escape liability if they had any nonracial reasons for their actions. Law and History Professors’ Brief as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
title: Comcast Corp. v. National Association of African American-Owned Media and Entertainment Studios Networks, Inc. (2020)
tags: Racial Discrimination, Civil Rights Law, 13th Amendment, 14th Amendment

description: Seven scholars with expertise in the history of criminal procedure filed a brief in Vega v. Tekoh, which ruled that a violation of the Miranda rule does not provide a basis for a lawsuit under the federal civil rights statute 42 U.S.C. § 1983. The brief argues that Miranda-like warnings were part of an Anglo-American legal tradition that the framers would have recognized. The amici examine 18th- and 19th-century British and American criminal court records to establish a practice of “giving warnings” to criminal suspects designed to curb “improper inducements” to self-incriminating confessions. The brief contends that this practice reflected a legal culture that “afforded very strong protections” to suspects subject to interrogation while in custody.
title: Vega v. Tekoh (2022)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Historians of Criminal Procedure in Support of Respondent
tags: Miranda Rights, Civil Rights, Fifth Amendment

description: Six historians of American sports filed a brief in National Collegiate Athletic Association v. Alston, which held that NCAA rules limiting how schools could compensate student athletes for their play violated federal antitrust law. The brief, in support of the student athletes, argues that the NCAA’s commitment to “amateurism in top-tier college sports is a myth.” Among other things, the amici survey the history of financial offers, favors, and payments in collegiate sports in the 19th and 20th centuries. Tag: Antitrust Law
title: National Collegiate Athletic Association v. Alston (2021)
brief_title: Brief of Historians as Amici Curiae Supporting Respondent

description: Ten legal historians filed a brief in Cedar Point Nursery and Fowler Packing Company v. Hassid, which ruled that a California regulation granting labor organizations a right to take access of an agricultural employer’s property to solicit support for unionization was unconstitutional under the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause. The brief, filed in support of the regulation, argues that Anglo-American law has never recognized an absolute right to exclude people from private property. The amici survey English common law, American colonial and state laws, and 18th- and 19th-century court cases to demonstrate a long tradition of making “limited rights to enter and exclude in the public interest part of the definition of property itself.”
title: Cedar Point Nursery and Fowler Packing Company, Inc. v. Hassid (2021)
brief_title: Brief of Legal Historians as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: Fifth Amendment, Takings Clause, Labor Unions

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Moore v. Harper, which rejected the so-called independent state legislature theory — a novel, fringe interpretation of the Constitution’s Elections Clause that would have allowed state legislatures to regulate federal elections without any of the traditional checks and balances on their lawmaking power. Ten scholars of early American history filed a brief to demonstrate that the independent state legislature theory is implausible as a historical matter. According to the amici, no evidence suggests that the framers believed in the theory, nor is it plausible that the framers would have endorsed it had they been presented with it. The brief emphasizes that the framers were wary of unchecked legislative power, and that they created the Elections Clause to limit out-of-control state legislatures. A scholar of the history of judicial review filed a brief challenging the independent state legislature theory. The brief explains that judicial review — including review of state legislation for compliance with state constitutions — was well established in the founding era and was implicit in the framers’ ideas of constitutionalism. Consequently, the brief concludes, the original meaning of the Elections Clause would permit state courts to review the laws that their legislatures make for federal elections.
title: Moore v. Harper (2023)
brief_title: Brief for Amici Curiae Scholars of the Founding Era in Support of Respondents | Brief of William M. Treanor as Amicus Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: Elections Clause, Elections, Democracy

description: The Supreme Court received multiple filings from historians in Trump v. Anderson, a case that reversed a Colorado state court ruling removing of Donald Trump from the state’s 2024 presidential primary ballot under Section 3 of the 14th Amendment. Four historians of federal constitutional amendments, the laws of war, and the Civil War and Reconstruction filed a brief arguing that the original intent, meaning, and public understanding of Section 3 supports Trump’s removal. According to the brief, Congress crafted Section 3 to ensure the republic’s security by automatically disqualifying any individual who engaged in an insurrection against the Constitution, including any insurrection that might occur after the Civil War, and barring from the presidency anyone who betrayed a constitutional oath. The amici couch their analysis in a historical narrative that begins with Lincoln’s election in 1860. Twenty-five historians of the Civil War and Reconstruction filed a separate brief supporting Trump’s removal. The brief surveys the history surrounding the ratification of the 14th Amendment to argue that Congress intended Section 3 to serve as “an enduring check on insurrection,” including insurrection carried out by the sitting president. The amici also argue that Section 3 is self-executing, requiring no additional congressional action once it had been enacted. A historian of the 20th Amendment filed a brief supporting Trump’s disqualification. The brief argues that the 20th Amendment’s original public meaning does not prohibit states from disqualifying a presidential candidate prior to an election and gives Congress no power to determine whether presidential candidates are qualified.
title: Trump v. Anderson (2024)

McPherson, Manisha Sinha, et al. as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents | Brief of Professor Edward J. Larson as Amicus Curiae Supporting the Anderson Respondents
tags: 14th Amendment, Elections, Democracy

description: Eight legal scholars and historians filed a brief in City of Grants Pass, Oregon v. Johnson, a case that upheld a city’s law regulating camping on public property against an Eighth Amendment challenge. The brief argues that the city’s attempts to enforce that law against people who are involuntarily homeless violates that amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishments. The amici maintain that the city’s law is not consistent with “a history and tradition of vagrancy laws.” They explain that the law differs in its purpose, scope, and structure from English and founding era vagrancy laws. In addition, they contend that the tradition of vagrancy laws contradicts modern understandings of liberty, equality, and decency, because such laws have historically been used to punish the poor and disfavored minorities and, after the Civil War, to subjugate formerly enslaved Black men and women.
title: City of Grants Pass, Oregon v. Johnson (2024)
brief_title: Brief of Professors William P. Quigley, Jeffrey Adler, Erwin Chemerinsky, Martha Davis, Helen Hershkoff, Stephen Loffredo, Nantiya Ruan, and Laurence H. Tribe as Amici Curiae in Support of Respondents
tags: Eighth Amendment

description: Nine scholars of tax law, legal history, and computational science filed a brief in Moore v. United States, a case that upheld the constitutionality of the mandatory repatriation tax. The brief, which supports the tax’s constitutionality, responds to the petitioners’ claim that the 16th Amendment did not authorize Congress to tax “unrealized” sums without apportionment among the states. Examining historical context relevant the original meaning of “incomes” in the text of the 16th Amendment, the amici conclude, among other things, that incomes included unrealized gains, and that contrary precedent should be overturned. They also critique assumptions by some corpus linguistics scholars that the 16th Amendment should be read in terms of its “ordinary usage in popular, nonlegal sources” rather than in a narrow, technical sense.
title: Moore v. United States (2024)
brief_title: Brief of Amici Curiae Professors of Tax Law, Legal History, and Computational Science in Support of Respondent
tags: 16th Amendment, Tax Law
